title: Hydroxide and hydronium
subtitle: Neutralisation: a proton moves from H₃O⁺ to HO⁻

reactants.caption: hydroxide + hydronium (Na⁺ and Cl⁻ are spectators)
reactants.learnerPrompt: Hydroxide meets hydronium. Draw the proton transfer.
hintTiers: Which species is electron-rich (the source of the arrow), and which carries an electron-poor hydrogen (the sink)?
A lone pair of hydroxide makes a new O–H bond. Hydrogen can hold only two electrons, so one O–H bond of H₃O⁺ breaks at the same time. Two arrows.
Arrow 1: a lone pair of hydroxide's oxygen to a hydrogen of H₃O⁺. Arrow 2: that hydrogen's old O–H bond onto the oxygen of H₃O⁺, which becomes water.

misconceptions.feedbackMessage: This arrow pushes electrons of H₃O⁺ towards hydroxide, which is already negative. Electrons flow from the electron-rich hydroxide to the proton.
The oxygen of H₃O⁺ carries the positive charge: it is the acid, not a source of electrons. Start from hydroxide.

partialProgressMessages.feedbackMessage: Good start: the lone pair makes a new bond to the hydrogen. But that hydrogen now has two bonds, four electrons, and it can hold only two. Which bond must break, and where do its electrons go?

water.caption: two water molecules (Na⁺ and Cl⁻ are spectators)

steps.explanationAfterStep: The strongest base that can exist in water takes a proton from the strongest acid that can exist in water. Every proton transfer needs two arrows: one makes the new bond to hydrogen, one breaks the old one.

mechanismSummary: The lone pair of hydroxide, the electron source, forms a bond to a hydrogen of H₃O⁺, the sink. At the same time the old O–H bond breaks and its electrons stay on oxygen. Two water molecules form; Na⁺ and Cl⁻ only watch.
references: Clayden, Greeves and Warren, Organic Chemistry, 2nd edition (Oxford University Press), chapter 8 (Acidity, basicity and pKa)
